# 037 · tableSizeFor rewritten with numberOfLeadingZeros, proved equal on all 2^32 inputs

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: equivalent on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`SymbolTable#tableSizeFor`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/rt/SymbolTable.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> The symbol table rounds a requested capacity up to a power of two with the five-shift bit smear of JDK 8's `HashMap.tableSizeFor`. A developer replaces the smear with the one-line form JDK 11 adopted, `-1 >>> Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(cap - 1)`. The regression proof compiles both versions into one program and proves them equal on every `int`, with the JDK's own bytecode of `numberOfLeadingZeros` in the proof.

Tags: [jvm-internals](../README.md#tag-jvm-internals), [numeric-code](../README.md#tag-numeric-code), [integer-overflow](../README.md#tag-integer-overflow)

## The change

Replace `n |= n >>> 1; n |= n >>> 2; ... n |= n >>> 16` with `-1 >>> Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(cap - 1)`: one intrinsic instead of five shifts and five ors, the same clamp to 1 and to the maximum capacity afterwards. It is the rewrite `java.util.HashMap` made in JDK 11. The tests for powers of two, rounding up and the ceiling all pass.

**Before** ([`SymbolTable.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/rt/SymbolTable.java), line 13):

```java

    /** The smallest power of two that is at least {@code cap}, between 1 and {@link #MAXIMUM_CAPACITY}. */
    public static int tableSizeFor(int cap) {
        int n = cap - 1;
        n |= n >>> 1;
        n |= n >>> 2;
        n |= n >>> 4;
        n |= n >>> 8;
        n |= n >>> 16;
        return (n < 0) ? 1 : (n >= MAXIMUM_CAPACITY) ? MAXIMUM_CAPACITY : n + 1;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java

    /** The smallest power of two that is at least {@code cap}, between 1 and {@link #MAXIMUM_CAPACITY}. */
    public static int tableSizeFor(int cap) {
        // Smear the highest set bit of cap - 1 downwards with one intrinsic instead of five shifts, as
        // HashMap.tableSizeFor does since JDK 11.
        int n = -1 >>> Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(cap - 1);
        return (n < 0) ? 1 : (n >= MAXIMUM_CAPACITY) ? MAXIMUM_CAPACITY : n + 1;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

For every input, the new code returns what the old code returned, or throws what it threw.

This is a proof over the whole domain (cap: int), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode of both versions and showed that it has no solution: no input exists on which they differ.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None if the two forms agree everywhere, and the edges are where they might not: `cap` of 0 and 1 (where `cap - 1` is 0 or negative and `numberOfLeadingZeros` returns 32 or 0), `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, and the values just over the maximum capacity. A table that comes out one bit too small overflows its mask and corrupts lookups; one that comes out as 0 or negative fails at allocation. A reviewer can check four edges by hand and does; the proof checks the other four billion.

## Why the verdict is right

The regression proof puts both versions of `tableSizeFor` in one program and asks JBMC whether any `int` makes them differ. `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros` is not a model: the tool puts the JDK's own `java.lang.Integer` class, read from the running JDK's image, on the solver's class path, so the proof is over the bytecode of the method as the JDK ships it (and so was the one in example 036 for `Math`). The solver finds no differing input in a fraction of a second, which is the proof: for all 2^32 capacities, the smear and the intrinsic produce the same power of two, with the same clamps. The property committed for the method (a power of two, at least the request, the smallest such, within the maximum) is proved of the new form as well.

## What to do

Merge. The proof is the review: the JDK's rewrite was correct in the JDK and it is correct here, and the next change to this method gets the same check against this version.

## Notes

- Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 1 method the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict. The recorded proof is JBMC's, which strict mode of the tool's own checker does not change; the checker refuses part of it in any mode (a static JDK method it does not model (java.lang.Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(int))). JBMC's own approximations are step 4c's.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 2 properties proved over cap: int in 0.3 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.
